rationale: A fixed 4% quorum with no participation safeguard let one bought stake in a dormant DAO pass a proposal alone and take the Timelock admin role. The attacker then became gov of the legacy UMA farms and used the gov-only escape hatch to withdraw their WETH and UMA, so the flaw is governance design rather than a code bug in the farms.

The private router authorizes multicall by its target and treats a target equal to itself as trusted, so a self-wrapped call reruns with the router's own identity and reaches a Safe module that trusts the router. The router and module are unverified, so the location is taken from the PoC and trace, and no Slither run covers the defect.

The vault's share price comes from Strategy.balanceOfY, which counts a Convex staked balance anyone can inflate through stakeFor and values the LP at the metapool's spot virtual price despite a depegged leg. The attacker deposited at the honest NAV, inflated it with cheaply minted LP, and withdrew at the inflated NAV; the delegatecall findings only point at the implementation hop.

The account proxy sets an 'initializable' flag in transient storage during construction, and initializeAccount checks only that flag, without an already-initialized guard. Transient storage lasts for the whole transaction, so in the same tx an attacker can re-initialize a freshly deployed, pre-funded account with a malicious bootstrap delegatecall and sweep it.

The shared UController's newOrganization is permissionless and trusts the reputation and token addresses that a caller-supplied avatar reports, reading them more than once. A shape-shifting fake avatar therefore registered the victim's real Reputation under an attacker-controlled organization, minted a voting majority and installed a scheme that drained the real Avatar; the contracts are unverified and Slither had no source.

For a first-time depositor, deposit() refunds part of the bonus-inflated amount at once and also credits token allocation that withdraw() later redeems for ETH. Nothing caps refund plus redemption at the ETH deposited, so a deposit and withdraw from each fresh address pays out more than it put in; the strict-equality findings are unrelated.

The module 'authenticates' a caller by asking that caller whether the module is enabled on it, so a fake Safe passes the check. It then makes a raw call to a caller-chosen router with caller-chosen calldata, which the attacker pointed at real Safes that had the module enabled, making them transfer out their collateral.

claimRewards adds the unaccounted ETH balance delta to totalRewards on every call, but updates lastETHBalance only when something is paid out. Calling it with an empty tokenIds array therefore counts the same donated delta again and again until one NFT can claim the whole pool; the uninitialized-local finding on claimable is not this weakness.

Settlement reads the hook pool's own instantaneous slot0 price with no TWAP or bound, puts the escrowed ETH back as liquidity around that price and runs a buyback with no price limit. Anyone can call accept() on an expired window, so the attacker moved the spot price with a flash loan, settled other users' windows, and swapped back through the misplaced ETH.

After a long idle period, the handler stores the whole inactive block gap on the first action of a block, and the interest model then charges that full gap on every later action in the same block at a utilization rate read from live totals. The attacker set that rate with flash-loaned deposits and borrows and withdrew the inflated deposit interest repeatedly; the proxy's delegatecall findings are just the forwarding layer, and the interest model has no Slither run.
